C0.quote: we study voting rules that are computable by querying voters about t < m candidates
C0.note: Computability and query complexity of positional scoring rules and STV.

C1.quote: fully characterizes the set of positional scoring rules that can be computed
C1.note: Characterisation and impossibility results (AX) plus query-complexity bounds (AL). Impossibility results are information-theoretic, so AX is primary.

C2.1.value: preference profile (distribution over rankings); preferences; rankings
C2.1.quote: A preference profile (or simply a profile) is a distribution σ over preferences

C2.2.quote: A ranking or preference over a set C of m candidates is a bijection
C2.2.note: Queries return rankings restricted to subsets of t candidates.

C2.3.quote: representing the underlying voter preferences that is unknown to the algorithm
C2.3.note: Voter preferences are referred to throughout, e.g. 'ordinal preferences'.

C2.4.quote: representing the proportion of voters in the population that have each ranking
C2.4.note: The profile is described as the voters' preferences. The rule is applied directly to it, with no discussion of submission or misreporting.

C3.1.note: No strategic voters are analysed. Sections checked: preliminaries, introduction, results, discussion.

C3.2.note: The paper does not state that voters submit their held preferences, either sincerely or truthfully.

C4.1.note: No voter utility, welfare or satisfaction notions are used. The 'score' is a rule score, not voter utility.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.note: Results concern computability of the winner and query complexity, not welfare, efficiency or representation of voters.

VOT.note: Voters are modelled as a distribution over rankings. They take no action in the model; the query algorithm samples from them.

CAN.note: Candidates are only alternatives to be chosen.

ORG.note: The query algorithm is a computational procedure, not an organiser choosing among strategic options. Under this codebook's definition, an organiser who chooses queries could arguably count, but the algorithm is analysed as a worst-case computational object.

C7.1.note: Fewer than two types are present.

C8.1.note: No type is STRAT or MIXED, so C8 is NA.

claims.quote: these results demonstrate the pitfalls of common rules like Plurality and STV
Primary elections in the United States, for example, routinely field large numbers of candidates

C9.1.note: The discussion draws practical implications about which rules are problematic under incomplete votes.

C9.2.quote: point to the space of alternative rules
C9.2.note: The claim about pitfalls of Plurality and STV in practice needs the assumption that elicited votes via random small queries reflect voters' held preferences. The paper does not state this. It also needs the assumption that the platform can sample voters from a fixed distribution.

C10.1.note: The paper does not say it studies the rule only as a function of submitted inputs, nor that it takes no position on how inputs relate to held attitudes.
